content: Congenital talipes equinovarus (CTEV), commonly referred to as clubfoot, is a congenital orthopedic condition characterized by an inwardly turned foot (equinovarus) and an abnormally high medial longitudinal arch (cavus). If left untreated, this condition can lead to long-term disability, deformity, and chronic pain. Treatment options for CTEV can be broadly categorized into conservative approaches, such as splinting or stretching, and surgical interventions. The effectiveness of these treatments may vary depending on the stage of presentation: at birth (initial presentation), when initial treatment fails (resistant presentation), when the condition recurs after initial success (relapse/recurrent presentation), or when no early treatment was provided (neglected presentation). This review aimed to evaluate the effects of any intervention for CTEV in individuals of any age. The search for relevant studies was conducted on May 28, 2019, across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Neuromuscular Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL Plus, AMED, and the Physiotherapy Evidence Database. Ongoing trials were also identified through the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform and ClinicalTrials.gov. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs comparing interventions for CTEV were included, with participants of all ages and presentations of CTEV. A total of 21 trials involving 905 participants were included in this review, with seven trials newly added since the last update. Fourteen trials focused on initial cases of CTEV (560 participants), four trials addressed resistant cases (181 participants), and three trials involved cases with unknown timing (153 participants). The heterogeneity of outcome measures across studies precluded data pooling for meta-analysis, even when interventions and participant characteristics were comparable. Most trials exhibited high or unclear risks of bias in at least three domains. Two trials assessed the primary outcome of function using validated scales, but the data could not be included due to unit-of-analysis issues and the unavailability of raw data for re-analysis. However, data on foot alignment, measured using the Pirani score (a scale ranging from 0 to 6, with higher scores indicating more severe deformity), were analyzed in three trials involving participants with initial presentation of CTEV. One trial demonstrated that the Ponseti technique significantly improved foot alignment compared to the Kite technique. After 10 weeks of serial casting, the average total Pirani score in the Ponseti group was 1.15 points lower than in the Kite group (mean difference [MD] −1.15, 95% confidence interval [CI] −1.32 to −0.98; 60 feet; low-certainty evidence). Another trial found the Ponseti technique to be superior to a traditional technique, with mean total Pirani scores 1.50 points lower in the Ponseti group after serial casting and Achilles tenotomy (MD −1.50, 95% CI −2.28 to −0.72; 28 participants; very low-certainty evidence). A third trial found no significant difference in foot alignment between casting materials used in the Ponseti technique, with semi-rigid fiberglass producing average total Pirani scores 0.46 points higher than plaster of Paris (95% CI −0.07 to 0.99; 30 participants; low-certainty evidence). No trials were identified that specifically addressed relapsed or neglected cases of CTEV. In a trial where the type of presentation was not reported, there was no evidence of a difference in foot alignment between an accelerated Ponseti technique and the standard Ponseti technique. At the end of serial casting, the average total Pirani score in the accelerated group was 0.31 points higher than in the standard group (95% CI −0.40 to 1.02; 40 participants; low-certainty evidence). Health-related quality of life was reported in some trials, but the data were not available for re-analysis. There was insufficient evidence to evaluate the addition of botulinum toxin A during the Ponseti technique, the effectiveness of different types of major foot surgery, or the use of continuous passive motion treatment following major foot surgery. Adverse events were infrequently reported. In trials evaluating serial casting techniques, adverse events included cast slippage requiring replacement, plaster sores, and skin irritation. Adverse events following surgical procedures included infections and the need for skin grafting. Two trials indicated that relapse after the Ponseti technique was more likely to be corrected with further serial casting, whereas relapse after the Kite technique more often required major surgery (risk differences of 25% and 50%, respectively). In conclusion, the Ponseti technique appears to result in significantly better short-term foot alignment compared to the Kite technique. However, the certainty of evidence is too low to draw definitive conclusions about its superiority over traditional techniques. An accelerated Ponseti technique may be as effective as the standard technique, but this finding is based on a single small trial. Semi-rigid fiberglass casting may be as effective as plaster of Paris when using the Ponseti technique. Relapse following the Kite technique more frequently necessitated major surgery compared to relapse after the Ponseti technique. The lack of validated outcome measures and the unavailability of raw data limit the conclusions that can be drawn from other included trials. Future RCTs should address these methodological issues to provide more robust evidence.
